recent_posts.title: The diminished art of coding
recent_posts.summary: A reflection on how AI coding agents are transforming programming from a craft into an assembly-line process. The author argues that LLMs have resolved the tension between code-as-art and code-as-function firmly in favor of function, shifting developer focus from low-level elegance to high-level architecture. The post encourages developers to seek artistic fulfillment outside of coding — through painting, music, dance, or fiction — as the human touch diminishes in software creation. It closes with the observation that we're in a 'fast-fashion era' of coding: software is vibe-coded, used, and discarded.

recent_posts.title: How programmers can find meaning in the age of AI coding tools
recent_posts.summary: A reflective narrative exploring the emotional journey of a programmer grappling with the rise of AI coding tools. Through a second-person story, it traces the arc from pride in hard-won technical mastery, through fear and resentment as AI democratizes software creation, to a potential path forward rooted in curiosity and creative purpose. The piece argues that the core reason most people got into programming — to build things and bring joy to others — remains unchanged, and that adapting with an open mind is more fulfilling than clinging to a threatened identity.

recent_posts.title: Maintaining wonder and skepticism in the age of AI coding agents
recent_posts.summary: AI coding agents have achieved remarkable feats recently—one-shotting browser APIs with 77% test pass rates, building rudimentary browsers, and creating C compilers that compile the Linux kernel. These accomplishments, unimaginable three years ago, deserve both wonder and skepticism. While tech optimists celebrate, it's important to acknowledge the extraordinary progress while also grieving what's been lost in the rapid technological shift. The key is maintaining both awe for innovation and critical awareness of its implications.

recent_posts.title: AI tools are ending programming as a craft
recent_posts.summary: AI coding tools are fundamentally changing software development, forcing developers to choose between moral principles and career survival. While AI can generate code faster and potentially better than humans, this shift transforms programming from a craft into code review and oversight. Senior developers face pressure to adopt these tools or risk being outpaced by junior colleagues using AI assistants. The transition marks the end of hand-coding as a craft, similar to how blacksmithing became obsolete, leaving experienced developers to mourn the loss of creative satisfaction and personal ownership in their work.

recent_posts.title: 15 years of blogging
recent_posts.summary: A reflection on 15 years of technical blogging, covering 151 posts across topics like Android, JavaScript, web performance, and accessibility. The author discusses the evolution from seeking readers to managing audience anxiety, highlights most popular posts (including "Safari is the new IE" and performance benchmarking work), and emphasizes that impact matters more than page views. The piece advocates for developers to blog regularly, be vulnerable in public, and use writing as a tool for thinking, despite fears of controversy or criticism.

recent_posts.title: Building a browser API in one shot
recent_posts.summary: An experiment demonstrates building a complete IndexedDB implementation from scratch using Claude AI with a single prompt and automated iteration loop. The implementation passes 95% of targeted Web Platform Tests and 77.4% of a more rigorous test suite, achieving results comparable to fake-indexeddb (82.8%) in just a few hours. The project cost approximately $7 and produced 4,395 lines of TypeScript code backed by SQLite. While the code quality is reasonable and the approach leverages Web Platform Tests as acceptance criteria, the author reflects on how AI tools are devaluing traditional software development efforts while acknowledging their inevitable dominance in the field.

recent_posts.title: AI tribalism
recent_posts.summary: A developer's perspective shift on AI coding tools over 2025, moving from skepticism to having 90% of code authored by Claude Code. The piece examines how debates around LLMs have become tribal and political, acknowledging both the genuine capabilities of modern AI coding assistants (bug detection, automated fixes, iterative improvements) and the uncertainty about software development's future. The author advocates for experimentation and empathy rather than entrenched positions, noting that while the technology has crossed a practical threshold, nobody truly knows where it's heading.

recent_posts.title: 2025 book review
recent_posts.summary: A personal reading list for 2025 covering historical fiction by Cecilia Holland (medieval tales of cultural clashes), philosophy (Marcus Aurelius' Meditations), science fiction (Roadside Picnic), and non-fiction about Silicon Valley ideology and Gandhi. The author reflects on slower reading habits due to gaming and a new job, sharing candid opinions on each book's pacing, themes, and personal relevance.

recent_posts.title: An experiment in vibe coding
recent_posts.summary: A developer built a travel itinerary web app using AI coding assistants (Bolt.new and Claude Code) with minimal manual coding. The experiment succeeded in creating a functional PWA with PocketBase backend for $21/month, but revealed limitations: AI tools aren't ready for non-programmers, generated code had accessibility issues and React performance problems requiring manual optimization, and token limits were frustrating. The experience highlights how AI-generated code works well for personal projects where requirements are simple and one user needs satisfaction, but remains unsuitable for professional codebases requiring team understanding and customer reliability.

recent_posts.title: Practical strategies for using AI coding agents effectively
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares practical strategies for using AI coding agents effectively after transitioning from skepticism to adoption. Key recommendations include creating comprehensive CLAUDE.md files for project context, using automated tests as feedback loops, running separate AI sessions for code review to catch bugs, and leveraging agents for overnight work on side projects. The author acknowledges AI's limitations with UI work and novel projects, describes the shift toward an architect-like role focused on specs and review, but maintains reservations about using AI for open-source contributions due to ownership concerns.
